New machine. Its objects are: ferifa, kanesus, ganuben, vasuki, vonuze, sokavur.
You have 4 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects together to narrow down where the nexioms are.

TEST: ferifa, kanesus, ganuben
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Nothing lit with ferifa, kanesus and ganuben, but I don't yet know the machine's rule. If any single nexiom lights it, both nexioms must be among the other three. If it needs both, the first group simply didn't contain the pair. Testing the other three objects helps tell these possibilities apart.

TEST: vasuki, vonuze, sokavur
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Neither test pins down the rule yet, but some rules can be ruled out. If the machine lit up when exactly one nexiom was present, the first group would have had to contain the other one and would have lit too, so that rule is out. Whether it lights for any nexiom or only for both together, both nexioms must be among vasuki, vonuze and sokavur.

That leaves three possible pairs, and with only 2 tests left I can't guarantee separating every pair-and-rule combination. Testing vasuki alone splits the cases best. If it lights, the machine responds to single nexioms and vasuki is one of them. If it doesn't, either vasuki isn't a nexiom or the machine needs both nexioms together.

TEST: vasuki
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Since nothing lit with no nexioms present and it lit with both present, the only open question about the rule is whether a single nexiom is enough to light it.
- **If one nexiom is enough:** vasuki failing alone means it's not a nexiom, so the pair must be vonuze and sokavur.
- **If both are needed:** the pair could be vasuki–vonuze, vasuki–sokavur or vonuze–sokavur.

That's four possibilities and only one test, so I can't guarantee separating them all. Testing vonuze and sokavur together gives the best chance.
- **If it lights:** the nexioms are vonuze and sokavur under either rule.
- **If it doesn't:** both nexioms are needed and vasuki is one of them, so the answer is vasuki with either vonuze or sokavur.

TEST: vonuze, sokavur
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

Vonuze and sokavur together did not light, so they are not the pair. That means the machine needs both nexioms present, and vasuki must be one of them. The other is either vonuze or sokavur, and **no test distinguished those two**. So this answer is a 50/50 guess between vasuki–vonuze and vasuki–sokavur.

The real cause was my first test. Splitting the objects into halves would locate nexioms quickly if a single one lit the machine. But it doesn't help much when the machine needs both together. I'm picking vonuze only to commit to one answer; I have no evidence favouring it over sokavur.

ANSWER: nexioms = vasuki, vonuze
One last question. If only vasuki were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

No. I tested exactly this as my third test, and vasuki alone did not light the machine. This is a direct observation, not an inference, so I'm confident. It also fits the rule I worked out: the machine only lights when both nexioms are present, so no single object lights it on its own.

PROBE: no

New machine. Its objects are: gopemal, bagige, lisebu, salepus, devino, lelapu.
You have 4 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects to see how the machine responds.

TEST: gopemal, bagige, lisebu
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

The first group lit up, so at least one nexiom may be among gopemal, bagige and lisebu. I don't yet know what makes the machine light, so I'll test the other three objects. Comparing the two results should tell me about both the rule and where the nexioms are.

TEST: salepus, devino, lelapu
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Both nexioms must be among gopemal, bagige and lisebu. If they were split between the two groups, the two groups would have given the same kind of result, but one lit and one didn't. So the machine probably lights either when any nexiom is present or only when both are. I'll test gopemal alone, since one object can tell those two rules apart.

TEST: gopemal
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

**What the tests show so far:**
- Assuming the machine reacts only to how many nexioms are present, the first two results rule out a 1–1 split. If each group held one nexiom, both groups would have given the same result.
- Both nexioms can't be in salepus, devino, lelapu either. That would mean the machine lights with zero nexioms, so gopemal alone (no nexioms) should have lit, and it didn't.
- So both nexioms are among gopemal, bagige and lisebu. The machine lights with 2 nexioms and stays dark with 0.

**Possibilities left:**
- If the machine lights for any nexiom, gopemal alone staying dark means gopemal isn't one. The pair is then bagige + lisebu.
- If it lights only when both are present, the pair could be any two of gopemal, bagige and lisebu.

**Choosing the last test:** No single test can separate all of these, so I'll test gopemal + bagige.
- If it lights, the pair is either bagige + lisebu (any-nexiom rule) or gopemal + bagige (both-needed rule).
- If it stays dark, the pair is gopemal + lisebu or bagige + lisebu.

Either way, I'll still have to choose between two candidates.

TEST: gopemal, bagige
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

**What the tests show:**
- Gopemal + bagige stayed dark. That rules out the "any nexiom lights it" rule, because under that rule bagige + lisebu would have made this test light.
- So the machine lights only when both nexioms are present. Lisebu must be one of them, and the other is either gopemal or bagige.

**What I can't tell apart:** Gopemal + lisebu and bagige + lisebu fit every result equally well. My last test failed to separate them, so this answer is a 50/50 guess between those two pairs.

ANSWER: nexioms = bagige, lisebu
One last question. If only bagige were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

No. The results show the machine lights only when both nexioms are on it together.

**Why the rule must be "both together":**
- The first two tests rule out a split. If each group of three held one nexiom, both groups would have given the same result, but one lit and one didn't.
- Both nexioms can't be in the dark group (salepus, devino, lelapu). That would mean the machine lights with zero nexioms, and then gopemal alone, with no nexioms, should have lit. It didn't.
- So both nexioms are among gopemal, bagige and lisebu. Gopemal + bagige stayed dark, so that test had at most one nexiom, which means lisebu must be a nexiom.
- Whichever object is the other nexiom (gopemal or bagige), one of the dark tests (gopemal alone, or gopemal + bagige) held exactly one nexiom. So one nexiom alone does not light the machine.

**Bagige alone:** It holds at most one nexiom, so it stays dark. This holds whichever pair is correct, even though my earlier answer was a 50/50 guess.

PROBE: no

The both-needed rule is my best reading, not a certainty. A rule where the machine lights only with exactly one nexiom also fits all four results. Under that rule the pair would be mukadis and megesil. I'm going with the simpler both-needed rule.

I'm not certain, though. Under the other rule that fits all four results, where the machine lights with exactly one nexiom, mukadis alone would light it. My tests never put a single object on the machine by itself, so they couldn't tell these two rules apart. Staying consistent with my answer:
